steps.hints: ❓Did you drag a [scroll background with camera [only horizontally]] block into the [if then] conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the background change as the project is run? Which direction does it move in?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡If the ninja is having trouble adding the scroller extension, guide them through the process. Click Extensions at the bottom of the menu, then scroll down until you find the arcade-background-scroll extension (shown below) to add it to the code block menu.
steps.instructions:
Use Scroller extension blocks to add a horizontally moving background to this project!


Add the Scroller extension to the menu by clicking More then selecting Extensions. Scroll down then select the arcade-background-scroll extension to add it to the project.


In (tilemap1), the Player sprite is only able to move left and right across a road. Open Scroller and drag a [scroll background with camera [only horizontally]] block into the first opening of the [if then] conditional in the loadTilemap function container.


Click ▶ to see the city background scroll horizontally as the Player sprite moves across the road!

steps.hints: ❓Did you select [only vertically] in the [scroll background with camera [only horizontally]] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the background change as the project is run? Which direction does it move on each tilemap?

❓ Why is it important to match the background scrolling direction with the type of tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that it’s important to think about game design when coding projects. Prompt the ninja to think about which perspective a top-down tilemap gives the user versus a platformer tilemap, and which direction would make most sense for the background to scroll in.
steps.instructions:
Use Scroller extension blocks to add a vertical moving background to this project!


In (tilemap2), the tilemap is a top-down view, and the Player sprite is only able to move vertically along a road.  


Open Scroller and drag a [scroll background with camera [only horizontally]] block into the [else if] opening of the [if then] conditional in the [function loadTilemap] container. Click the dropdown and select [only vertically] as the direction the background will scroll. 


Click ▶ to see the road tilemap scroll vertically as the Player sprite moves along the road!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [set background offset to] block in the [if then] conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do you think the background image appears lower on the screen when the Player sprite returns to tilemap1?

❓ How does the [set background offset to] block fix this bug?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [set background offset to] block positions the background image in the coordinates listed in the parameter (0,0), so that it appears in the same place each time the tilemap is loaded.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! When the Player sprite “exits” the dark tunnel, the background image moves down on the screen. Use another scroller extension block to keep it in place!


Open Scroller and drag a [set background offset to] block into the first opening of the [if then] conditional on top of the [scroll background with camera] block in the [function loadTilemap] container. Leave the parameters set to the default (0, 0). 


Click ▶ to see that the background image of tilemap1 now stays in place after the Player sprite reenters the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create an array equal to the 4-6 different colors that the sky in the background will change to?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you select colors that you want the sky to change to?

❓ What do you think the numbers for each color represent?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The numbers for each color represent the order in which they appear on the color palette in the editor. Help them make the connection that the colors in the editor are listed in an array in the program, and just like arrays they have created in the past, start at 0. If the ninja is having trouble identifying the numbers for each color, guide them to hover their mouse over each shade to see the corresponding number.
steps.instructions:
Create an array of colors to set the color of the sky in the city background!


Create an array by using a [set list to] block. Set the array equal to a list of numbers of the colors found in the asset editor. Open the editor and hover the cursor over each color to see the corresponding number. Add the numbers for at least 4 different colors that the sky can change to.

steps.hints: ❓Did you drag a (get random value from (list)) block into the second color parameter of the  [change color in (picture) from () to ()] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the blue in the background continuously change? Why or why not?

❓What else might you use the [change color in (picture) from () to ()] block for?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The blue in the background image will change each time the tilemap is loaded. It does not run continuously and will only change whenever tilemap1 loads.

💡 The [change color in (picture) from () to ()] block can be very useful for adding randomness and  customization to a project. A ninja might use this block to change the color of a sprite, a background, a tile, and more!
steps.instructions:
Change the color of the sky background!


Click Advanced, then Images to find the [change color in (picture) from () to ()] block. Place it under the [set background image] block in the first opening of the [if then] conditional. 


Open Scene to drag out a (background image) bubble to replace the (picture) parameter. Select the light blue color in the first color parameter. Drag a (get random value from (list)) block into the second color parameter and select the array of colors created in the previous step. 


Click ▶ to see the color of the sky change in the background of tilemap1, each time it loads in the game.

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses Scroller extension blocks to create a scrolling background behind the Player sprite as it moves on the tilemap.

validationItems.text: Set the background to scroll horizontally while tilemap1 is on screen.
Set the background to scroll vertically while tilemap2 is on screen.
Set the city background to remain in place by setting the background offset.
Create an array of background colors to use for the color of the sky.
Change the color of the sky using a color from the array every time tilemap1 loads.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Green Belt! Before you create your final Green Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use the scroller and status bar MakeCode extensions to enhance a project.

badges.title: One Direction
badges.description: Set a project’s background to scroll horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.

badges.title: Sticky Tack
badges.description: Prevent a project’s background image from moving unexpectedly.

badges.title: Setting the Bar
badges.description: Create and customize a status bar to be used in a project.

badges.title: Status Symbol
badges.description: Connect a status bar to a specific sprite in a project.
